subskill: form: pronoun-antecedent and subject-verb agreement (split object pronoun)
passage: A small lunar probe lost its main antenna during its final week of operation. Although the probe's last status report, a single burst sent on the final reserve of battery power, reached Earth clipped and scrambled by solar interference, the radio engineers at both tracking stations ______ from the partial recording made at each receiving dish. Their reconstruction shows the probe tumbling slowly toward the surface.
explanation: The verb's subject is the plural "engineers" ("the radio engineers at both tracking stations"), not the singular "probe's" or "report" in the opening clause, so the verb is "have reconstructed." What the engineers reconstructed is the opening clause's "last status report," named almost thirty words before the blank and singular, so the pronoun is "it"; "burst" renames that same report. "Have reconstructed them" carries the verb's plural number onto the pronoun, but the plural nouns near the blank, "engineers" and "stations," are the reconstructors and their workplaces, not the thing rebuilt. "Has reconstructed it" and "has reconstructed them" pair a singular verb with the plural "engineers."

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement and verb tense (habitual whenever-clause)
passage: Over three summers, two glaciologists photographed the front of a tidewater glacier at hourly intervals from a ridge above its fjord. Undercut by warm currents and split by crevasses, the glacier's calving front ______ to collapse in slabs the height of a building whenever the meltwater lakes that pool on the upper ice in midsummer drain through cracks to the bed. The photographs captured more than forty such collapses.
explanation: The subject is the singular "front" ("the glacier's calving front"); "currents" and "crevasses" belong to the opening participial phrase, so the verb is singular. The tense is set by the habitual clause "whenever the meltwater lakes that pool on the upper ice in midsummer drain through cracks to the bed": its verbs "pool" and "drain" are present (the past would be "pooled" and "drained"), and a present habitual clause requires a present main verb, so "is prone" is correct. "Was prone" follows the past narration around it ("photographed," "captured"), but a past main verb cannot govern a present "whenever" clause. "Are prone" and "were prone" are plural, agreeing with "crevasses" or "lakes" rather than with "front," and "were prone" also clashes with the present clause.
topic_tag: glaciology: calving at a tidewater glacier front

subskill: boundaries: semicolon between independent clauses (delayed verb)
passage: Inspectors load-testing a new steel footbridge photographed each weld on the underside of its deck. One photograph caught two defects near the north abutment: an orange rust stain and a faint gray ______ fainter mark along the lowest weld of the main girder tore open under the heaviest load two days later. The span stayed closed until that girder was replaced.
explanation: The words after the blank form a complete clause: its subject is "the fainter mark along the lowest weld of the main girder," and its verb, "tore," arrives eleven words after the blank, so two independent clauses meet at the blank. With no conjunction, they are joined by a semicolon. A comma reads "the fainter mark ..." as an appositive renaming "line" until "tore" arrives, and then leaves a comma splice. A colon is ruled out because the sentence already uses its colon after "abutment" to introduce the two defects, and a sentence takes only one colon; no mark at all fuses the two clauses.
topic_tag: structural engineering: hairline cracks in footbridge welds

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement and verb aspect (definite past vs present perfect)
passage: Wind-blown dust that settles on a telescope's mirror scatters part of the starlight that would otherwise reach the camera. With the dome closed against the wind, the primary mirror's hexagonal segments ______ with jets of carbon dioxide snow by two engineers on the evening of the observatory's yearly open house. The cleaned mirror gathers several percent more light than it did beforehand.
explanation: The subject is the plural "segments"; "dome" belongs to the opening phrase and "mirror's" only modifies the head, so the verb is plural. The phrase "on the evening of the observatory's yearly open house" pins the cleaning to one particular occasion, and a specific point in time takes the simple past, not the present perfect, so "were cleaned" is correct. "Have been cleaned" is plural and tempts because the cleaned mirror "gathers" more light now, but the present perfect cannot be tied to a named occasion such as "the evening of the ... open house." "Has been cleaned" makes the same error with a singular verb, and "was cleaned" is singular, agreeing with "dome" or "mirror's" rather than with "segments."
topic_tag: observational astronomy: dust on telescope mirror segments

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement and auxiliary choice (cataphoric ellipsis)
passage: Whereas the steel tapes of nineteenth-century survey crews ______, a tape of invar, an alloy of iron and nickel, barely lengthens in summer heat. Crews working with steel corrected each baseline measurement for the air temperature, a chore that invar made largely unnecessary. That stability made invar tapes standard equipment for measuring the baselines of national surveys.
explanation: The blank stands in for a verb that the main clause supplies later: the steel tapes lengthen, so the elided verb is the present lexical verb of "barely lengthens in summer heat," and an elided present lexical verb is represented by a form of "do." The subject of the opening clause is the plural "tapes," so "do" rather than "does." "Does" tempts because the main clause's subject, "a tape of invar," is singular and its verb is "lengthens," but that noun belongs to a different clause. "Was" and "were" are forms of "be," which cannot stand in for "lengthens"; the historical setting of "nineteenth-century survey crews" makes them attractive, but the main clause offers no form of "be" for them to echo.
topic_tag: geodesy: thermal expansion of surveying tapes

subskill: form: pronoun-antecedent and subject-verb agreement (split object pronoun)
passage: Meteoroids no bigger than pebbles burn up high in the atmosphere, but they can chip the solar panels of satellites in low orbit. Given that grains this small are too dim for the optical cameras on survey telescopes, the radar receiver beside the observatory's twin domes ______ through the faint trails of ionized gas that streak the upper atmosphere at dawn. Its operators send the nightly counts to satellite controllers.
explanation: The verb's subject is the singular "receiver"; "domes" is part of the phrase "beside the observatory's twin domes," so the verb is "is tracking." What the receiver tracks is named at the start of the sentence, "grains this small," a plural noun more than twenty words before the blank, so the pronoun is "them" even though the verb is singular. "Is tracking it" copies the subject's singular number onto the pronoun, but the receiver cannot be the object of its own verb and no singular noun in the sentence is being tracked. "Are tracking them" and "are tracking it" make the verb plural, agreeing with "domes" rather than with "receiver."
topic_tag: meteor science: radar counts of pebble-sized meteoroids

subskill: boundaries: comma after an introductory dependent clause (garden path, late position)
passage: Engineers widening a mountain highway had to cut back a limestone ridge that overhung the road. As the crew ______ loosened boulders on the slopes above the valley road fell across both lanes, and the highway stayed closed for a week. The contractor later anchored steel netting over the slopes.
explanation: The introductory clause is "As the crew blasted the ridge": "the ridge" is the object of "blasted," and the main clause's own subject, "loosened boulders on the slopes above the valley road," follows, with its verb, "fell," ten words after the blank. A comma sets the introductory dependent clause off from the main clause, so it belongs after "ridge." A comma after "blasted" makes "the ridge loosened boulders on the slopes above the valley road" a complete main clause, which reads well until "fell" is left with no subject. With no comma, the same misreading ("the ridge loosened boulders") runs the clause's object into the main clause, and a semicolon cannot separate a dependent clause from the clause it introduces.
topic_tag: highway engineering: rock blasting above a mountain road

subskill: form: subject-verb agreement and verb tense (past progressive passive)
passage: A blast furnace is relined only once in fifteen years or so, and the work is usually done in stages so that the plant can keep producing iron. The copper staves in the lower wall of the furnace's hearth ______ by welders in heat-resistant suits while the refractory bricks lining the shaft overhead slowly cooled to a dull red.
explanation: The subject is the plural "staves"; "wall" and "hearth" sit inside the phrase that locates them, so the verb is plural. The tense is set by the while-clause, whose own verb comes only at its end: "lining" is a participle, and the finite verb is "cooled," fifteen words after the blank, which places the work in the past and requires the past progressive "were being replaced." "Are being replaced" is plural but present; it tempts because the first sentence describes relining as a present process and "lining" reads as present, yet it cannot run alongside the past "cooled." "Was being replaced" is past but singular, agreeing with "hearth," and "is being replaced" is wrong in both number and tense.
topic_tag: metallurgy: relining a blast furnace hearth

subskill: form: possessive noun (singular possessive decided by another sentence)
passage: The only shelter on one volcano's crater rim was a hut with a single bunk, and each page of the logbook kept there is signed in the same hand. The ______ sketches the hut's summer visitors found pinned to its walls show the lava lake's crust splitting and sinking in a regular cycle.
explanation: The word before "sketches" must name their owner, and the first sentence implies there was exactly one: the hut had "a single bunk," and each page of its logbook "is signed in the same hand," so one observer lived there and made the sketches: "observer's." "Observers'" would credit several people; the plural "summer visitors" makes it tempting, but the visitors only found the sketches. "Observer" lets "sketches" read as a verb ("The observer sketches the hut's summer visitors"), a sentence that seems complete until "found" and "show" are left with no place in it. "Observers" is a plain plural that neither shows possession nor agrees with "sketches" read as a verb.
topic_tag: volcanology: a lone observer's lava lake sketches

subskill: boundaries: semicolons in a series whose later item contains commas
passage: The comet probe, launched on a small rocket, weighed less than a family car. Built of aluminum, titanium, and carbon fiber, its science deck held a magnetometer at the tip of a folding ______ dust counter angled to catch the grains streaming off the comet's nucleus; and a narrow-angle camera, the heaviest instrument aboard. Each instrument drew power from two solar wings.
explanation: The blank separates the first two items in a series of three instruments. The third item, "a narrow-angle camera, the heaviest instrument aboard," contains its own commas, so every item in the series must be separated by a semicolon. A comma would be right only in a series whose items contain no commas, like "aluminum, titanium, and carbon fiber" earlier in the same sentence; here it would blur where one instrument ends and the next begins. A colon cannot divide two items within a list, and no mark runs "boom" into "a dust counter."
topic_tag: planetary missions: a comet probe's instrument deck
